title: Fiber Architecture & Reconciliation
description: Fiber tree linked-list traversal, double buffering, reconciliation diffing, key anti-patterns, and concurrent time-slicing.

subtopics.title: Fiber Tree & Linked List Traversal
subtopics.summary: Child, Sibling, Return pointers, current vs workInProgress trees, and double buffering.
subtopics.mentalModel: React 16+ models UI as a singly linked list of Fiber nodes rather than a recursive tree. Each fiber has `child`, `sibling`, and `return` (parent) pointers. During updates, React clones the `current` tree into a `workInProgress` tree (double buffering) and switches the pointer during the synchronous commit phase.
subtopics.traps: Believing reconciliation is immediate/synchronous; forgetting that the render phase can be paused, aborted, or restarted in Concurrent Mode.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: In React's Fiber reconciler, every React element is represented by a Fiber Node — a mutable unit of work with linked-list pointers (`child`, `sibling`, `return`) that enables depth-first tree traversal without recursive call stack frames.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Define a factory function `createFiberNode(tag, pendingProps, key)`.
Initialize structural linked-list pointers: `child = null`, `sibling = null`, `return = null` (parent pointer).
Initialize state and work tracking properties: `stateNode = null`, `type = null`, `memoizedProps = null`, `memoizedState = null`.
Initialize reconciler flags and lane scheduling: `flags = 0`, `subtreeFlags = 0`, `alternate = null` (for double buffering).
Return the constructed Fiber node.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React source code (`packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js`), the `FiberNode` constructor creates these exact fields. Pointers replace the DOM tree hierarchy with a singly-linked list structure, enabling interruptible work loops.

complexity.time: O(1) constant time allocation per Fiber node.

edgeCasesHandled: Null or missing keys default to `null`.
Correct initialization of both `pendingProps` and null `memoizedProps`.
Correct pointer defaults for tree linking.

specifications: React Architecture Docs: A Deep Dive into React Fiber (Andrew Clark)
verifiedRules: Fiber trees use child, sibling, and return pointers to represent hierarchical relationships.
Every fiber maintains an alternate pointer pointing to its counterpart during work.

questions.title: Iterative Fiber Depth-First Walker
questions.concept: Non-Recursive Tree Traversal via Fiber Pointers
questions.problemStatement: Implement `walkFiberTree(root, onVisit)` that visits every node in a Fiber tree in depth-first order using ONLY `child`, `sibling`, and `return` without recursion or array stacks.
questions.interviewTrap: Using recursion will overflow the call stack when React reconciles large DOM trees of 10,000+ nodes.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React reconciles component trees using an iterative Depth-First Search (DFS) walker through `child`, `sibling`, and `return` pointers. This eliminates recursive function calls, enabling the work loop to pause at any node and resume later.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Accept root fiber node `root`.
Initialize `current = root` and an array `visited = []`.
While `current !== null`:
1. Record `visited.push(current)` (beginWork phase).
2. If `current.child !== null`, descend: `current = current.child` and continue loop.
3. If no child, we complete the work (completeWork phase). While `current !== null`:
a. If `current.sibling !== null`, traverse laterally: `current = current.sibling` and break to step 1.
b. Otherwise, ascend up to parent: `current = current.return`.
c. If we return to root or above, terminate.
Return `visited` sequence.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: This algorithm is the exact core of React's `workLoopSync` and `workLoopConcurrent` (`packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`). `beginWork` descends down `child` pointers, and `completeWork` bubbles up `return` pointers while pivoting across `sibling` pointers.

complexity.time: O(N) visiting each fiber node in the tree exactly twice (once on descent, once on ascent).
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary call stack space (strictly iterative pointer traversal).

edgeCasesHandled: Single root node without children returns `[root]`.
Deep unbalanced trees traverse without call stack overflow.
Multi-child sibling chains traverse in correct left-to-right order.

specifications: Lin Clark's A Cartoon Intro to Fiber (DFS work traversal explanation)
verifiedRules: Child pointer is visited first; if absent, sibling is visited; if absent, return pointer is ascended.
The traversal is strictly O(1) in call stack memory.

questions.title: Fiber Double Buffering (WorkInProgress Tree Cloner)
questions.concept: Double Buffering & Pointer Flipping in Commit Phase
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createWorkInProgress(currentFiber, pendingProps)` that creates or reuses the `alternate` Fiber node. It must clone the current node into its alternate, update `pendingProps`, link their mutual `alternate` references, and return the workInProgress node.
questions.interviewTrap: Re-allocating new objects on every render causes GC churn. React reuses the existing `current.alternate` node whenever available to maintain peak performance.

testCases.testFn: const current = { tag: 'Host', type: 'div', memoizedProps: {}, alternate: null }; const wip = createWorkInProgress(current, { id: 'wip' }); return current.alternate === wip && wip.alternate === current;

testCases.name: Reuses existing alternate on subsequent renders (zero new object allocation)
testCases.testFn: const current = { tag: 'Host', type: 'div', memoizedProps: {}, alternate: null }; const wip1 = createWorkInProgress(current, { count: 1 }); const wip2 = createWorkInProgress(current, { count: 2 }); return wip1 === wip2 && wip2.pendingProps.count === 2;

testCases.name: Updates pendingProps while preserving memoizedProps until commit
testCases.testFn: const current = { tag: 'Host', type: 'div', memoizedProps: 'old', alternate: null }; const wip = createWorkInProgress(current, 'new'); return { pending: wip.pendingProps, memoized: wip.memoizedProps };

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React utilizes a Double Buffering pooling strategy to avoid constant object allocations during re-renders. At any time, there are at most two trees: the `current` tree (rendered on screen) and the `workInProgress` (WIP) tree (being constructed in memory). They mirror each other via `alternate` pointers.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Implement `createWorkInProgress(current, pendingProps)`.
Check if `current.alternate` already exists:
- If `null`, instantiate a new Fiber node `workInProgress`, set `workInProgress.alternate = current` and `current.alternate = workInProgress`.
- If `alternate` exists (from previous render pass), recycle it! Copy updated `pendingProps`, reset `flags = 0`, `subtreeFlags = 0`, and copy over pointers.
Ensure `workInProgress.child = current.child`, `workInProgress.memoizedProps = current.memoizedProps`, etc.
Return recycled or newly allocated `workInProgress` fiber.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js`, `createWorkInProgress` recycles existing fibers instead of allocating new JS objects on every render. This dramatically reduces V8 Heap garbage collection churn during frequent updates (e.g. 60fps animations or typing).

complexity.time: O(1) constant time per fiber clone/recycle operation.
complexity.space: O(1) auxiliary allocation (reuses alternate fiber once instantiated).

edgeCasesHandled: Initial render creates alternate and binds bidirectional link (`a.alternate = b` and `b.alternate = a`).
Subsequent renders reuse existing alternate object without GC allocation.
WorkInProgress resets mutation flags to clean slate.

specifications: React Architecture Docs: Double Buffering in Fiber Reconciler
verifiedRules: At most two fiber instances exist per component across all render passes.
The alternate pointer points bidirectionally between current and workInProgress.

subtopics.title: Diffing Algorithm & The 'key' Prop Trap
subtopics.summary: O(n) heuristic diffing, element type comparison, key stability, and index-as-key state corruption.
subtopics.mentalModel: React diffs level-by-level with 2 assumptions: elements with different types produce different trees, and keys uniquely identify siblings across renders. If element types differ, the entire subtree is unmounted and rebuilt from scratch.
subtopics.traps: Using array index as key when list items can be reordered, inserted, or filtered (leads to state attached to wrong inputs/components).

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React's list reconciliation algorithm requires unique, stable `key` props on array children to identify which items have changed, been added, or been removed. Missing keys or duplicate keys trigger console warnings and cause severe DOM diffing bugs.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Accept an array of React element children.
Initialize `seenKeys = new Set()` and diagnostic result object `{ missingCount: 0, duplicates: [] }`.
Iterate over children:
- If child has no `key` property (or `key === null` or `key === undefined`), increment `missingCount++`.
- If child has a key, check if `seenKeys.has(child.key)`: if already seen, push `child.key` to `duplicates`; else `seenKeys.add(child.key)`.
Return diagnostic report.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js`, `reconcileChildrenArray` checks keys. If a key is missing, React warns in development. If keys are duplicated, React logs a warning and cannot guarantee which child will retain state or receive DOM updates.

complexity.time: O(N) single linear scan over children array.
complexity.space: O(N) Set storage for distinct keys.

edgeCasesHandled: All unique keys report 0 missing and 0 duplicates.
Missing keys correctly tallied.
Multiple duplicates of the same key captured without crashing.

specifications: React Official Docs: Preserving and Resetting State (Rules of Keys)
verifiedRules: Keys must be unique among siblings.
Missing keys disable optimal child matching and force linear fallback diffing.

questions.title: Key-Based List Reconciler (Minimal DOM Operations)
questions.concept: O(n) Sibling Diffing using Key Maps
questions.problemStatement: Implement `reconcileChildren(oldChildren, newChildren)` that matches old and new list items by `key`. Returns `{ reused: string[], created: string[], deleted: string[] }`.
questions.interviewTrap: Without keys, React falls back to index comparison. Inserting an item at the beginning causes ALL subsequent items to re-render and mutate.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React's list diffing reconciler transforms an old list of children into a new list with minimal DOM mutations. Using a Map keyed by `key`, React matches existing nodes in O(N) time and tracks a `lastPlacedIndex` to determine which nodes only need to be moved versus created or deleted.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Build a hash map of existing children: `existingMap = new Map(oldChildren.map(c => [c.key, c]))`.
Initialize `operations = []` and `lastPlacedIndex = 0`.
Iterate through `newChildren` with index `i`:
- If `existingMap.has(newChild.key)`:
Retrieve `oldChild = existingMap.get(newChild.key)` and `existingMap.delete(newChild.key)`.
If `oldChild.index < lastPlacedIndex`, record `MOVE` operation!
Else update `lastPlacedIndex = oldChild.index`.
- Else: record `INSERT` operation for `newChild`.
Any nodes remaining in `existingMap` were not reused: record `DELETE` operation for each.
Return calculated operations list.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: This algorithm in `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js` (`mapRemainingChildren` & `placeChild`) solves the tree edit distance problem in O(N) time instead of the theoretical O(N^3) general tree diffing minimum.

complexity.time: O(N + M) linear time where N is old list length and M is new list length.

edgeCasesHandled: Reordering items (e.g., reversing or shifting) produces minimal MOVE operations.
Adding new items produces INSERT operations.
Removing items generates DELETE operations for unvisited keys.

specifications: React Architecture Docs: Reconciliation Diffing Algorithm
verifiedRules: List reconciliation completes in O(N) linear time using key-based mapping.
lastPlacedIndex tracks relative ordering to minimize DOM node relocations.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Using array indices as keys (`key={index}`) is a notorious React anti-pattern. When items are inserted, deleted, or reordered, an item's index changes. React compares components by key; if keys remain `0, 1, 2...`, React matches the old index 0 fiber to the new index 0 item, preserving the old fiber's internal state (uncontrolled inputs, stateful hooks) on the WRONG data!
stepByStepWalkthrough: Simulate state corruption caused by index keys during item deletion or unshift.
Detect if `key === index` pattern is being used on stateful components.
Diagnose: When an item is prepended or deleted, component at index 0 retains old internal state because key `0` matched.
Remediate: Replace index keys with stable entity IDs (e.g. `item.id`).
Verify that with stable ID keys, component state remains strictly attached to the correct logical entity across reorders.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: During reconciliation, React uses `(element.key === null ? element.type : element.key)` to find matching fiber nodes in `alternate`. Matching an index key matches the old Fiber node whose `memoizedState` linked list contains the previous item's state values, leading to visual bugs and form input corruption.

complexity.space: O(N) memory for item state tracking.

edgeCasesHandled: Deleting first item with index keys corrupts last item's display.
Migrating to stable ID keys restores 100% state fidelity.
Preserves input field cursor and focus state.

specifications: Robin Pokorny: Index as a key is an anti-pattern (Cited in official React docs)
React Official Docs: Why keys are needed and why indices fail
verifiedRules: Index keys break component state identity when lists are modified.
Stable unique IDs guarantee that Fiber node memoizedState stays bound to the correct entity.

subtopics.title: Render Phase vs Commit Phase Mechanics
subtopics.summary: Pure render functions, side effects placement, synchronously flushing DOM changes in commit phase.
subtopics.mentalModel: The Render Phase calls component functions and reconciles virtual fibers. It MUST be pure with zero side effects, because React may abort or restart it multiple times. The Commit Phase applies DOM changes synchronously, then runs layout and passive effects.
subtopics.traps: Mutating global variables, making network calls, or setting state inside the render function body.

questions.subtopicTitle: Render Phase vs Commit Phase Mechanics

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React's pipeline is divided into two distinct phases: The **Render Phase** (pure computation, diffing, finding changes) and the **Commit Phase** (applying changes to the host DOM and executing side-effects). A Pure Component Render Inspector checks whether component functions remain pure and side-effect free during the render phase.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Accept a component render function and props.
Instrument global environment to intercept side-effects (e.g. DOM mutations, global variable writes).
Invoke the component render function twice (simulating React's `<StrictMode>` double-render in development).
Compare the two outputs: both renders must return identical element trees without mutating external state.
Report any detected impurities or differences.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React Concurrent Mode, the Render Phase can be paused, aborted, restarted, or thrown away if higher-priority work arrives. If a component performs side-effects (e.g. `window.count++`) during render, those side-effects execute unpredictably multiple times.

complexity.time: O(R) where R is the render execution time of the component.

edgeCasesHandled: Pure functions pass with zero flagged side-effects.
Impure side-effects during render (mutating external state) are detected.
StrictMode double-rendering simulation verifies determinism.

specifications: React Official Docs: Keeping Components Pure
React Source: ReactStrictMode.js (Double-invoking component renders in dev)
verifiedRules: Render phase must be pure and free of observable side effects.
Side effects must be deferred strictly to the commit phase (useEffect / useLayoutEffect).

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Simulating a complete Two-Phase Render and Commit Pipeline shows how React computes an effect list during render, and then executes synchronous DOM mutations and lifecycle commits in the commit phase.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Phase 1: Render Phase (`renderRoot`)
- Traverse component tree, compute new virtual representation, and diff against current state.
- Accumulate mutation flags (`Placement`, `Update`, `Deletion`) onto fiber nodes without touching the real DOM.
Phase 2: Commit Phase (`commitRoot`)
- Synchronously iterate through fibers with effect flags.
- Sub-phase 1: Before Mutation (getSnapshotBeforeUpdate).
- Sub-phase 2: Mutation (DOM insertions, deletions, updates).
- Sub-phase 3: Layout (useLayoutEffect synchronous execution).
- Flip double buffer root pointer: `root.current = workInProgress`.
- Schedule passive effects (useEffect) asynchronously.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js`, `commitMutationEffects` mutates the DOM tree synchronously in one uninterrupted batch. This ensures the browser never renders an inconsistent intermediate UI state.

complexity.time: O(N) render diffing + O(M) commit mutations where M is number of changed fibers.

edgeCasesHandled: Render phase can abort without affecting DOM if work is canceled.
Commit phase executes in strict sub-phase order.
Root alternate pointer flips atomically at the conclusion of commit.

specifications: Dan Abramov: Component Lifecycle / Render vs Commit Phases chart
verifiedRules: Commit phase is synchronous and un-interruptible.
DOM mutations occur exclusively within commitMutationEffects.

questions.title: Interruptible Work Loop with Time-Slicing Simulation
questions.subtopicTitle: Render Phase vs Commit Phase Mechanics
questions.problemStatement: Implement `runWorkLoop(workUnits, deadlineMs)` that processes an array of work units. It checks elapsed time after each unit, and if `deadlineMs` is exceeded, pauses execution, yields control, and returns `{ done: false, remainingCount }`. If all units finish within budget, returns `{ done: true, remainingCount: 0 }`.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React Concurrent Mode's core capability is Time-Slicing. Instead of a synchronous loop that blocks the thread until entire trees are processed, `workLoopConcurrent` yields control back to the browser host when the allotted frame deadline expires (`shouldYield()`), resuming in the next idle slice.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Implement `workLoopConcurrent(deadline)`:
Maintain global `workInProgress` pointer.
Loop `while (workInProgress !== null && !shouldYield())`:
`workInProgress = performUnitOfWork(workInProgress)`.
Check `shouldYield()`: if `performance.now() >= deadline.timeRemaining()`:
Pause loop, preserve current `workInProgress` pointer on the root scheduler, and schedule next slice via `MessageChannel` / `scheduler`.
Once `workInProgress === null` (all units complete), proceed to synchronous `commitRoot()`.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `packages/scheduler/src/forks/Scheduler.js` and `ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`, React uses a 5ms frame slice (via `MessageChannel.port1.postMessage`) to yield control back to the browser event loop for inputs, scrolling, and CSS animations.

complexity.time: O(N) total work across multiple yielded time slices.
complexity.space: O(1) stack space; state preserved in heap-allocated fiber pointers.

edgeCasesHandled: Yields when time slice expires without losing traversal position.
Short tasks complete within a single time slice without unnecessary yields.
High priority interruptions can discard incomplete workInProgress trees.

verifiedRules: Concurrent work loop checks shouldYield() before each unit of work.
Frame deadline defaults to 5ms to maintain 60-120fps responsiveness.
